case_name: Ross v. Board of School Trustees, District No. 15
text:
New Brunswick Court of Appeal

Citation: Attis c. Board of Education of District 15 et
al.
*

Court File: 27/92/CA

Date: 1993-12-20

Hoyt C.J.N.B., Angers and Ryan JJ.A.

Counsel:

Douglas H. Christie,
for appellant.

Joseph E. Weir,
for respondent, David
Attis.

Joanne E. McLeod,
Q.C., and
Thomas S.
Kuttner,
for respondent, Human Rights Commission.

Joel Richler,
for respondent, Canadian
Jewish Congress.

Gabriel Bourgeois,
for intervener,
Attorney-General of New Brunswick.

[
1
]

HOYT C.J.N.B.:—This is an appeal from a decision of Paul Creaghan
J. in the Court of Queen's Bench in which he set aside a portion of an order of
a board of inquiry that was established on September 1, 1988, pursuant to
s. 20

of the
Human Rights Act,
R.S.N.B. 1973, c. H-11. The Minister of Labour
constituted Brian D. Bruce as a board of inquiry to investigate a complaint
made by David Attis on April 21, 1988, against the board of School Trustees of
District No. 15.

[
2
]

Mr. Attis, a Moncton resident, who, in his complaint, described
himself as a Jew, alleged that the school board discriminated against three of
his children and other Jewish students, because of their religion or ancestry,
with respect to educational facilities and services available to the public,
contrary to s. 5(1) of the
Human Rights Act.
Section 5(1) provides:

5(1) No person, directly or indirectly, alone or with another,
by himself or by the interposition of another, shall

(
a
)

deny to any person or class of persons any
accommodation, services or facilities available to the public, or

(
b
)

discriminate against any person or class of
persons with respect to any accommodation, services or facilities available to
the public,

because of race, colour, religion, national origin, ancestry,
place of origin, age, physical disability, mental disability, marital status,
sexual orientation or sex.

Mr. Attis alleged that the discriminatory conduct by the school
board occurred from March 29, 1977, to April 21, 1988, and arose from the
actions of Malcolm Ross, a teacher employed by the school board, who taught at
its Magnetic Hill School. The gist of Mr. Attis' complaint is as follows:

By its own statements and its inaction over Malcolm Ross'
statements in class and in public, the School Board has condoned his views, has
thus provided a racist and anti-Jewish role model for its students, has
fostered a climate where students feel more at ease expressing anti-Jewish
views, and has reduced the credibility of the content of its official history
curriculum, thus depriving Jewish and other minority students of equal
opportunity within the educational system that the School Board provides as a
service to the public.

[
3
]

The impugned conduct was that Mr. Ross made racist and
discriminatory statements to his students and in published writings and one
public television appearance. In his published writings, which consist of four
books or pamphlets published from 1978 to 1989 and three letters to New
Brunswick newspapers, one of which took the form of a self-interview, Mr. Ross
argues that western Christian civilization is being undermined and destroyed by
an international Jewish conspiracy. As Creaghan J. noted, there can be little
doubt that Mr. Ross sincerely holds these views.

[
4
]

The hearing before Professor Bruce was lengthy. Because the
complaint was against the school board, there was considerable evidence
concerning its dealings with Mr. Ross resulting from his writings. At the time
of the hearing, Mr. Ross did not have a homeroom class, but was a modified
resource teacher at the Magnetic Hill School. He had been employed there since
September 30, 1976. Before that, he had been employed by the school board as a
teacher at the Birchmont School.

[
5
]

As early as 1978, concerns about Mr. Ross' writings were being
expressed publicly and, as well, concerns were expressed to the school board,
including a letter from the chairman of the Human Rights Commission in that
year, in which he requested that Mr. Ross' class-room performance be
supervised. By 1987, the school board's response to the controversy had become
a public issue. The New Brunswick Department of Education became involved.

[
6
]

In 1988, the school board instituted disciplinary action against
Mr. Ross. On March 16, 1988, Mr. Ross was reprimanded and warned that continued
public discussion of his views could lead to further disciplinary action,
including dismissal. He was informed that this warning also applied to
out-of-school activities. The reprimand remained in force until September 20,
1989. On November 21, 1989, Mr. Ross made the television appearance noted
earlier and, as a result, was again reprimanded by the school board on November
30, 1989.

[
7
]

As noted, Mr. Attis filed his complaint against the school board
with the Human Rights Commission on April 21, 1988. The complaint was
investigated by the commission. Because the commission could not resolve the
dispute, it recommended to the Minister of Labour that a board of inquiry be
set up to investigate Mr. Attis' complaint.

[
8
]

Mr. Attis' daughter Yona, a student attending another school in
School District No. 15, and Leigh Lambert, another Jewish student, testified
before the board that they were the subject of anti-Jewish remarks and actions
at their school. Yona Attis also testified that she was frightened when she had
occasion in 1988 to attend a gymnastics event at the Magnetic Hill School where
Mr. Ross taught. Mr. Attis was concerned that Mr. Ross' continued employment by
the school board would detrimentally affect the type of education his children
would receive as well as their emotional well-being. Ernest Hodgson, an educator,
testified that Mr. Ross' out-of-school activities could negatively impact
students within the school district.

[
9
]

Professor Bruce found that there was no evidence "of any
direct classroom activity by Malcolm Ross on which to base a complaint under
Section 5 of the Act". Professor Bruce then went on to consider Mr. Ross'
out-of-school activities in the following context:

Most of the evidence presented related to alleged
discriminatory actions by Malcolm Ross while off-duty which it is claimed had
the effect of creating a poisoned learning environment within School District
15 for Jewish parents and students. This evidence consists largely of public
statements and published writings by Malcolm Ross and resultant media coverage.
It is not alleged that any of the public statements and published writings were
carried out as part of Malcolm Ross' assigned school duties. However, it is to
be noted that a teacher's off-duty conduct can impact on his or her assigned
duties and thus is a relevant consideration.

An important factor to consider, in determining if the
Complainant has been discriminated against by Malcolm Ross and the School
Board, is the fact that teachers are role models for students whether a student
is in a particular teacher's class or not. In addition to merely conveying
curriculum information to children in the classroom, teachers play a much
broader role in influencing children through their general demeanour in the
classroom and through their off-duty lifestyle. This role model influence on students
means that a teacher's off-duty conduct can fall within the scope of the
employment relationship. While there is a reluctance to impose restrictions on
the freedom of employees to live their independent lives when on their own
time, the right to discipline employees for conduct while off-duty, when that
conduct can be shown to have a negative influence on the employer's operation
has been well established in legal precedent.

Professor Bruce found that Mr. Ross' off-duty comments
denigrated the faith and beliefs of Jews. He said:

These comments denigrate the faith and beliefs of Jews and
call upon true Christians to not merely question the validity of Jewish beliefs
and teachings but to hold those of the Jewish faith and ancestry in contempt as
undermining freedom, democracy and Christian beliefs and values. Malcolm Ross
identifies Judaism as the enemy and calls on all Christians to join the battle.

Professor Bruce went on to find that Mr. Ross' actions violated
s. 5(1) of the
Human Rights Act
and that there was no reasonable excuse
to justify the discriminatory effect of those actions.

[
10
]

Professor Bruce concluded that the school board, although not
intending to discriminate, did so, by failing to discipline Mr. Ross
meaningfully. By its almost indifferent response to the complaints and by
continuing his employment, the school board endorsed his out-of-school
activities and writings. As a result, there was an atmosphere where anti-Jewish
sentiments flourished and where Jewish students were subject to a "poisoned
environment" within the school district "which has greatly interfered
with the educational services provided" to Mr. Attis and his children.

[
11
]

Professor Bruce made a two-part order. First, he ordered the New
Brunswick Department of Education to modify its curriculum to accommodate
Holocaust studies. Secondly, he ordered that Mr. Ross be removed from his
teaching duties and, further, that if the school board continued his employment
on a non-teaching basis, he be prohibited from expressing anti-Jewish sentiments.
The portion of the order removing Mr. Ross from the class-room was based on
Professor Bruce's conclusion that Mr. Ross, as a teacher, was a role model and
thus subject to such a remedy.

[
12
]

The text of the order is as follows:

(1) That the Department of Education:

(a) establish an annual review process to set goals and to
assess progress in the implementation of the initiatives set out in the
Ministerial Statement on "Multicultural/Human Rights Education";

(b) develop in collaboration with school trustees and teachers
a system of periodic appraisals of the overall quality of race relations in the
school environment and procedures for responding to any discriminatory
situations identified;

(c) encourage all school boards to implement a policy which
will clearly establish the commitment of each board and teachers within that
board to teach respect for individual rights and tolerance of differences; and,

(d) review the
Schools Act
in consultation with the New
Brunswick Teachers' Association to determine whether it would be appropriate to
define within it a clear statement as to the level of professional conduct
expected of teachers in the Province of New Brunswick.

(2) That the School Board:

(a) immediately place Malcolm Ross on a leave of absence
without pay for a period of eighteen months;

(b) appoint Malcolm Ross to a non-teaching position if, within
the period of time that Malcolm Ross is on leave of absence without pay, a
non-teaching position becomes available in School District 15 for which Malcolm
Ross is qualified. The position shall be offered to him on terms and at a
salary consistent with the position. At such time as Malcolm Ross accepts
employment in a non-teaching position his leave of absence without pay shall
end.

(c) terminate Malcolm Ross' employment at the end of the
eighteen month leave of absence without pay if, in the interim, he has not been
offered and accepted a non-teaching position.

(d) terminate Malcolm Ross' employment with the School Board
immediately if, at any time during the eighteen month leave of absence or if at
any time during his employment in a non-teaching position, he:

(i) publishes or writes for the purpose of publication,
anything that mentions a Jewish or Zionist conspiracy, or attacks followers of
the Jewish religion, or

(ii) publishes, sells or distributes any of the following
publications, directly or indirectly:

•
Web of Deceit

• The Real Holocaust
(
The
Attack on Unborn Children and Life Itself
)

• Spectre of Power

•

Christianity vs.
Judeo-Christianity
(
The Battle for Truth
)

[
13
]

Mr. Ross sought judicial review of Professor Bruce's decision [
1991 CanLII 8194 (NB QB)
, 86
D.L.R. (4th) 749,
1991 CanLII 12118 (NB QB)
, 16 C.H.R.R. D/250, 121 N.B.R. (2d) 361]. Paul Creaghan J.,
who heard the application, quashed, because there "was no
jurisdiction", ss. 1 and 2(d) of the order. In addition, the judge found
that s. 2(d) of the order violated
s. 2
of the
Canadian Charter of Rights
and Freedoms
,
and could not be saved by
s. 1
of the Charter. The quashed
portions of the order related to the Department of Education and the gag order
against Mr. Ross. The judge, however, upheld those portions of the order that
removed Mr. Ross from the class-room, namely,
s. 2
(a), (b) and (c). He
concluded that although Mr. Ross'
s. 2(
a
) and (
b
)

Charter
rights were "impinged" by s. 2(a), (b) and (c) of the order,
s. 2(a)
,
(b) and (c) were saved by s. 1 of the Charter.

[
14
]

In upholding s. 2 (a), (b) and (c) of the order, Paul Creaghan J.
said [at p. 758]:

There are two central criteria that must be satisfied. First,
the thrust of s. 5 of the
Human Rights Act
must be of sufficient
importance to warrant overriding the protected constitutional rights. Second,
the order of the board of inquiry must meet the test of proportionality, that
is, it must be reasonable and demonstrably justified.

The order of the board of inquiry must be rationally connected
to the objective of rectifying the cause and effect of the violation of the
Human
Rights Act.
Further, the order should impair as little as possible the
constitutional rights in question. Lastly, the effect of the order which limits
Mr. Ross' constitutional rights must be proportional, that is, reasonable and
demonstrably justified, with respect to the importance of the objective of s. 5
of the
Human Rights Act.

My analyses of the direction of the Supreme Court of Canada in

Oakes
upon the facts of this case leads me to the conclusion that the
finding of the board of inquiry and els. 2 (a), (b) and (c) of its order are
saved as a reasonable limit prescribed by law as can be demonstrably justified
in a free and democratic society pursuant to
s. 1
of the
Charter
.

[
15
]

Mr. Ross' submissions on this appeal are that Professor Bruce's
award was patently unreasonable, that he erred in certain rulings made during
the hearing, that portions of the
Human Rights Act
are contrary to the
Canadian
Charter of Rights and Freedoms

and that the remedy imposed by Professor
Bruce infringed Mr. Ross' right to freedom of expression as guaranteed by
s. 2

of the Charter. Mr. Attis, the Human Rights Commission and the Canadian Jewish
Congress have all cross-appealed, submitting that the gag order quashed by Mr.
Justice Creaghan should be reinstated. The Province of New Brunswick has
intervened, submitting that portions of the
Human Rights Act
are not
contrary to the Charter.

[
16
]

Although it is not relevant to this decision, I would note that
while the complaint was directed against the school board, it is Mr. Ross who
stands to be penalized.

[
17
]

Because, in my view, the
Charter
argument determines the appeal,
I will deal only with it.

[
18
]

Sections 1
,
2(
a
) and (
b
)

of the
Charter

provide:

1. The
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms

guarantees
the rights and freedoms set out in it subject only to such reasonable limits
prescribed by law as can be demonstrably justified in a free and democratic
society.

2. Everyone has the following fundamental freedoms:

(
a
) freedom of conscience and religion;

(
b
)

freedom of thought, belief, opinion and
expression, including freedom of the press and other media of communication;

[
19
]

There can be little doubt that, as Paul Creaghan J. found, s.
2(a), (b) and (c) of Professor Bruce's order offends Mr. Ross' s. 2(
a
)
and (
b
)

constitutional rights to freedom of conscience, religion
and expression. For publicly expressing his sincerely held views, Mr. Ross was
penalized by being prevented from continuing his teaching career.

[
20
]

The issue is somewhat easier to state than to resolve. Is this
sanction demonstrably justifiable in a free and democratic society? The issue
is whether an individual's freedom of expression can prevail against the fear
that there will be a public perception that Mr. Ross' discriminatory remarks
directed against a religious or ethnic minority are being condoned. The
discrimination here is aggravated because the minority is one that has been
historically targeted for discrimination and because the author of the
discrimination is a teacher, who might be considered a role model to students.

[
21
]

Before testing the order against
s. 1
of the
Charter
, I will
briefly deal with Mr. Ross' submission that s. 21 of the
Human Rights Act
is
contrary to the provisions of the Charter and therefore of no force and effect.
Section 21 of the
Human Rights Act
provides:

21(1) All orders and decisions of a Board of Inquiry are final
. . .

Counsel for the Attorney-General concedes, and I agree, that a
decision of a board of inquiry that violates a
Charter
right is subject to
judicial review notwithstanding s. 21 of the
Human Rights Act.
Accordingly,
s. 21 does not offend the Charter.

[
22
]

Paul Creaghan J. examined the order in the context of
Charter
guarantees
and found that Mr. Ross' freedoms of expression and religious belief were
violated by Professor Bruce's order, but concluded that the portion of the
order that removed Mr. Ross' from class-room teaching could be saved by
s. 1
of
the Charter. As stated earlier, Mr. Ross' submission is that s. 2(a), (b) and
(c) of the order cannot be saved by s. 1 of the Charter and, therefore, must be
quashed.

[
23
]

There is no doubt that a teacher may be disciplined for off-duty
activities. In
Cowichan School Trustees of School District #65 v. Peterson
(1988),

1988 CanLII 2942 (BC CA)
, 22 B.C.L.R. (2d) 98, 8 A.C.W.S. (3d) 164 (C.A.), a teacher was suspended for 12
months for being sexually intimate with a young former student. In
Re
Etobicoke Board of Education and Ontario Secondary School Teachers' Federation,
District 12
(1981),
1981 CanLII 4445 (ON LA)
, 2 L.A.C. (3d) 265, a teacher was dismissed after being
found guilty of conspiracy to possess stolen goods. In
Shewan v. Abbotsford
School District No. 34
(1986),
1986 CanLII 879 (BC SC)
, 26 D.L.R. (4th) 54, 70 B.C.L.R. 40 (S.C.), a
teacher whose nude photograph appeared in a magazine and her teacher husband
who took the photograph were suspended for six weeks. In
Abbotsford,
Bouck
J. reviewed cases, some involving teachers, where off-duty conduct was the
subject of discipline: see also
Eraser v. Canada
(
Public Service
Staff Relations Board
)

(1985),
1985 CanLII 14 (SCC)
, 23 D.L.R. (4th) 122, [1985] 2 S.C.R.
455, 63 N.R. 161. In none of these cases, however, was an employee's
Charter

right alleged and found to have been violated. Although
Eraser
involved
freedom of expression, the events giving rise to the dismissal occurred before
the Charter had been proclaimed.

[
24
]

To use the analysis set out in
R. v. Oakes
(1986),
1986 CanLII 46 (SCC)
, 26
D.L.R. (4th) 200, 24 C.C.C. (3d) 321, [1986] 1 S.C.R. 103, we must determine if
the silencing of Mr. Ross' anti-Semitic views is such an important public
objective that his constitutional rights to freedom of expression and speech
can be overridden. Paul Creaghan J., as noted, was of the view that it was. In
my opinion, the recent decision of the Supreme Court of Canada in
R. v.
Zundel
(1992),
1992 CanLII 75 (SCC)
, 95 D.L.R. (4th) 202, 75 C.C.C. (3d) 449, [1992] 2 S.C.R.
731, a decision not available to Paul Creaghan J., although dealing with the
false news provision in the
Criminal Code
,
bears on the issue here.
Writing for the majority, McLachlin J. said at p. 267: "Justification
under s. 1 . . . requires a specific purpose so pressing and substantial as to
be capable of overriding the
Charter
's guarantees." Therefore, the purpose
of the order being reviewed here, namely, Mr. Ross' removal from the
class-room, must be "so pressing and substantial" before the
constitutional guarantee of freedom of expression can be overridden by
s. 1
of
the Charter. Viewed in that context and considering the evidence, it is my
opinion that the order cannot stand.

[
25
]

Professor Bruce found that Mr. Ross did not attempt to further
his views in the class-room. No connection was made between Mr. Ross' expressed
views and any offensive remarks directed to Miss Attis and Mr. Lambert. Remarks
made by school-children in the playground of another school are, in my opinion,
too tenuous to found such a restriction. If the evidence disclosed that Mr.
Ross' remarks sparked or even were used to legitimize the offensive remarks
made in the school-yard, perhaps the sanction in the order would be
appropriate.

[
26
]

It must be remembered that it was Mr. Ross' activities outside
the school that attracted Mr. Attis' complaint. The evidence does not disclose
that Mr. Ross ever used or contended that he was free to use his teaching
position to further his religious views. Nor did he suggest that the school
board acquiesced in his views. True, he was a teacher and, as such, his views
may be thought to have an authority they might not otherwise achieve. Mr. Ross'
position as a teacher, and thus a role model, is central to Professor Bruce's
order. Teachers do indeed enjoy a high status in our society and have a unique
opportunity to influence youthful minds. Having said that, however, the
sanction, curtailment of Mr. Ross' freedom of expression, must be considered in
the context of the evidence. As noted, it has never been suggested that he used
his class-room or school property to further his views.

[
27
]

In such circumstances, I do not conclude that this remedy, which
violates Mr. Ross' constitutional guarantee of freedom of expression, meets the
requirement of being "a specific purpose so pressing and substantial"
that the guarantee should be overridden. To hold otherwise would, in my view,
have the effect of condoning the suppression of views that are not politically
popular at any given time. Perhaps I am giving too much weight to the
"slippery slope" fear expressed by Dickson C.J.C. in
R. v.
Keegstra
(1990),
1990 CanLII 24 (SCC)
, 61 C.C.C. (3d) 1 at p. 51, [1990] 3 S.C.R. 697, 1 C.R.
(4th) 129. In my opinion, however, the denial of an individual's freedom of
expression can only occur in the clearest of cases. In my view, the evidence
does not disclose that this case meets that test.

[
28
]

For the above reasons, I would allow the appeal and remove s.
2(a), (b) and (c) of Professor Bruce's order of September 28, 1991, into this
court and quash the said subsections. I would dismiss the cross-appeals. As Mr.
Ross did not request costs, I would make no order of costs.

[
29
]

ANGERS J.A. concurs with Hoyt C.J.N.B.

[
30
]

RYAN J.A. (dissenting):—The pertinent question in this case is
whether an elementary schoolteacher, Malcolm Ross of Moncton, whose position is
found to be that of a role model, can be prohibited by an order of a human
rights board of inquiry from publicly expressing discriminatory anti-Semitic
sentiments. At issue are (1) freedoms of expression and religion when in
conflict with (2) a prohibition against discrimination. Are the rights to these
two freedoms absolute?

[
31
]

A one-person board of inquiry, Brian D. Bruce, professor of law
at the University of New Brunswick, Fredericton, held that Ross' discriminatory
statements and published writings outside the class-room were such that they
had to be muted. Professor Bruce also found that the responsibility for
discipline lay with the Board of School Trustees for School District No. 15. He
held that the school board failed in that responsibility.

The school hoard

[
32
]

Although Professor Bruce went on to find that the school board
failed in its responsibility, he did point out some of the corrective action
taken by the school board:

A television interview which Malcolm Ross gave in 1989 gives
further insight into his motives and purpose for writing. This Board of Inquiry
agrees with the characterization which the School Board gave to the interview
when it ordered Malcolm Ross to refrain from publicly assailing and denouncing
another religion. The School Board went on to state that in its view ". .
. the climate created by this aggressive approach creates hostility that
permeates and interferes with the desired tolerance required by the school
system to show respect for the rights of all students and their families to
practice their religious faith." This Board of Inquiry has no hesitation
in concluding that the public statements and writings of Malcolm Ross have
continually over many years contributed to the creation of a poisoned
environment within School District 15 which has greatly interfered with the
educational services provided to the Complainant and his children.

[
33
]

Professor Bruce concluded that the school board was in breach of

s. 5
of the
Human Rights Act,
R.S.N.B. 1973, c. H-11:

5(1) No person, directly or indirectly, alone or with another,
by himself or by the interposition of another, shall

(
а
)
deny to any person or class of persons any accommodation, services or
facilities available to the public, or

(
b
) discriminate against any person or class of persons
with respect to any accommodation, services or facilities available to the
public,

because of race, colour, religion, national origin, ancestry,
place of origin, age, physical disability, mental disability, marital status,
sexual orientation or sex.

[
34
]

Professor Bruce looked at the responsibility of the school board
with respect to acts in the workplace. He criticized the inaction of the school
board and the failure of a review committee to address the questions which it
ought to have addressed. He said that in accepting the review committee report,
the school board failed to appreciate the necessity of addressing the larger
picture and the difficult issue of assessing the subtle forms which
discrimination can take.

Malcolm Ross

As for Ross, Professor Bruce said:

This Board of Inquiry has no hesitation in concluding that
there are many references in these published writings and comments by Malcolm
Ross which are prima facie discriminatory against persons of the Jewish faith
and ancestry. It would be an impossible task to list every prejudicial view or
discriminatory comment contained in his writings as they are innumerable and
permeate his writings. These comments denigrate the faith and beliefs of Jews
and call upon true Christians to not merely question the validity of Jewish
beliefs and teachings but to hold those of the Jewish faith and ancestry in
contempt as undermining freedom, democracy and Christian beliefs and values.
Malcolm Ross identifies Judaism as the enemy and calls on all Christians to
join the battle.

He said that the writings and comments of Ross could not be
categorized as coming within the scope of scholarly discussion. With respect to
Ross' off-duty conduct he said:

On a review of all of the evidence and circumstances
surrounding Malcolm Ross' off-duty conduct in relation to his published
statements and writings, it is the conclusion of this Board of Inquiry, on the
balance of probabilities, that the actions of Malcolm Ross have violated
Subsection 5(1) of the
Act
and there is no reasonable cause to excuse
the discriminatory effect of these actions.

[
35
]

As a further illustration of the intensity of Ross' attacks,
Professor Bruce cited from one of Ross' letters: "My whole purpose in
writing and publishing is to exalt Jesus Christ and to inform Christians about
the great Satanic movement which is trying to destroy our Christian faith and
civilization." Professor Bruce continues:

Further on in the letter he quotes what he claims is biblical
support for claiming that Jews are the synagogue of Satan. His encouragement of
others to condemn Jews and throw off the
"yoke
of Jewish
domination" is assisted through referring to Judaism as teaching that
". . . Jesus Christ is a bastard, a lewd deceiver, a false prophet who is
burning in Hell." He further claims that Judaism teaches that the Virgin
Mary is a whore. Malcolm Ross concludes his articles by indicating that he
intends to continue his research, writing and publishing.

The board of inquiry

[
36
]

I accept the principle that under the human rights legislation of
the province persons constituted as boards of inquiry are experts in a
specialized field of identifying "discrimination" and in dealing with
it. Subject to a
Charter
challenge, I accept Professor Bruce's finding that:

Although there was no evidence that any of the students making
anti-Jewish remarks were directly influenced by any of Malcolm Ross' teachings,
given the high degree of publicity surrounding Malcolm Ross' publications it
would be reasonable to anticipate that his writings were a factor influencing
some discriminatory conduct by the students.

[
37
]

With respect to the school board's responsibility, Professor
Bruce went on to hold as follows:

This Board of Inquiry would, having reviewed all of the
evidence, conclude on the balance of probabilities that the School Board has
discriminated against the Complainant contrary to Subsection 5(1) of the
Act

and there is no reasonable cause to excuse the discriminatory effect. The
reasons have been summarized above and a reading of these will indicate that
generally this Board found no evidence of any intent to discriminate. The
effect, however, on the Complainant and his children is one which a reasonable
person would anticipate resulting from the actions of the School Board
particularly the failure to address the Malcolm Ross issue in any meaningful
way prior to 1988.

The impugned order

[
38
]

The order made by Professor Bruce is in two parts. The first part
relates to the Department of Education and commands the department to do
certain things such as the legislature of the province might order. This was
quashed on judicial review by Mr. Justice PS. Creaghan as being in excess of
jurisdiction [
1991 CanLII 8194 (NB QB)
, 86 D.L.R. (4th) 749,
1991 CanLII 12118 (NB QB)
, 16 C.H.R.R. D/250, 121 N.B.R. (2d) 361]. I
agree. The second part of the order was subdivided into four parts. The first
three, (a), (b) and (c), were upheld by Mr. Justice Creaghan. He held that
although they violated
s. 2
of the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
,
they
were saved under
s. 1
as being a reasonable limit which he held had been
demonstrably justified; (a), (b) and (c) are as follows:

(2) That the School Board:

(a) immediately place Malcolm Ross on a leave of absence
without pay for a period of eighteen months;

(b) appoint Malcolm Ross to a non-teaching position if, within
the period of time that Malcolm Ross is on leave of absence without pay, a
non-teaching position becomes available in School District 15 for which Malcolm
Ross is qualified. The position shall be offered to him on terms and at a
salary consistent with the position. At such time as Malcolm Ross accepts
employment in a non-teaching position his leave of absence without pay shall
end.

(c) terminate Malcolm Ross' employment at the end of the
eighteen month leave of absence without pay if, in the interim, he has not been
offered and accepted a non-teaching position.

Malcolm Ross was promptly given a non-teaching position.

[
39
]

Creaghan J. quashed s-s. (d) as violating rights to freedom of
speech and religion under
s. 2
of the
Charter
. He held that it could not be
saved under s. 1 as had been (a), (b) and (c). Here is the subsection that was
struck:

(2) That the school board:

• • • • •

(d) terminate Malcolm Ross' employment with the School Board
immediately if, at any time during the eighteen month leave of absence or if at
any time during his employment in a non-teaching position, he:

(i) publishes or writes for the purpose of publication,
anything that mentions a Jewish or Zionist conspiracy, or attacks followers of
the Jewish religion, or

(ii) publishes, sells or distributes any of the following
publications, directly or indirectly:

•
Web of Deceit

• The Real Holocaust
(
The
Attack on Unborn Children and Life Itself
)

•

Spectre of Power

•

Christianity vs.
Judeo-Christianity
(
The Battle for Truth
)

Discrimination

[
40
]

The
Human Rights Act
of New Brunswick prohibits
discrimination under s. 5(1). The board of inquiry, a specialized board to
which we are required to give deference, has found discrimination by the school
board against the complainant because of the school board's failure to take
appropriate action against Malcolm Ross. The finding of discrimination is
therefore, in the circumstances of this case, unassailable. However, there is
no curial deference if the order is contrary to a provision in the
Charter
.

[
41
]

Ross, as a schoolteacher is a role model to pupils in an
elementary school, inside and outside the class-room. He teaches developing
minds. He is a role model to children and yet, outside the class-room, he
advocates prejudice. He urges discrimination. He publicly proclaims outside the
class-room that which would not be tolerated if said in the class-room. He is a
servant of the public. In my opinion, a teacher cannot discriminate, in the
sense of show bias, inside the class-room or publicly, in such an important
area as is this target in the
Human Rights Act
of this province.

[
42
]

Anti-discrimination is a laudable goal. It is an important
provincial aim. In this case, can it withstand the test in head-to-head combat
with
s. 2
of the
Charter
which protects free speech, conscience and religion?

Section 2
is as follows:

2. Everyone has the following fundamental freedoms:

(
a
) freedom of conscience and religion;

(
b
)

freedom of thought, belief, opinion and
expression, including freedom of the press and other media of communication;

(
c
)

freedom of peaceful assembly; and

(
d
)

freedom of association.

Is free speech an absolute?

[
43
]

In a 1985 case, Chief Justice Dickson said that "freedom of
speech" was a deep-rooted value in our democratic system of government. In

Fraser v. Canada
(
Public Service Staff Relations Board
)

(1985),

1985 CanLII 14 (SCC)
, 23 D.L.R. (4th) 122, [1985] 2 S.C.R. 455, 9 C.C.E.L. 233, he said that it is a
principle of our common law Constitution, inherited from the United Kingdom by
virtue of the preamble to the
Constitution Act, 1867
.
The Chief Justice
said that freedom of speech was not an absolute value and that probably no
values are absolute. Speaking for a unanimous court, he said that all important
values must be qualified and balanced against other important, and often
competing, values. With the interposition of
s. 2
of the
Charter
, has the value
and effect of this pronouncement changed? Is it outdated?

[
44
]

If anything, the deep root is fortified because it is now
entrenched in the Constitution. In
R. v. Oakes

(1986),
1986 CanLII 46 (SCC)
, 26 D.L.R. (4th)
200, 24 C.C.C. (3d 321, [1986] 1 S.C.R. 103, Chief Justice Dickson said at p.
225 that rights under the
Charter
are not absolute, that it "may become
necessary to limit rights and freedoms in circumstances where their exercise
would be inimical to the realization of collective goals of fundamental
importance".

[
45
]

The right to be free from discrimination is not rooted merely in
provincial legislation. It might be said to be
quasi
-constitutional from
a provincial perspective but it is aided by
s. 2
itself of the
Charter
: the
right to be free from discrimination in religion, thought and speech. Inherent
in the evilness of discrimination is an outright attack on the freedoms of
others protected under
s. 2
by persons urging their own freedoms as though
there were no consequences to the exercise of them.

[
46
]

Therefore, as I see it, both values must be weighed. Is the competing
value, that of prohibiting discrimination, sufficiently consequential in this
case that the rights of free speech and freedom of religion should be qualified
as ordered by the board of inquiry? I am of the opinion that they can be and
should be, similar to situations where the right runs head-on into laws dealing
with libel and slander, sedition and blasphemy, restrictions on the press in
order to ensure a fair trial or to protect minors or victims of sexual assault.

The Oakes test

[
47
]

On judicial review, Creaghan J. distinguished between the
Charter

perspective of Ross in the class-room as compared to that outside the
class-room. He quoted from
R. v. Oakes
,
at p. 225:

The court must be guided by the values and principles
essential to a free and democratic society which I believe embody, to name but
a few, respect for the inherent dignity of the human person, commitment to
social justice and equality, accommodation of a wide variety of beliefs,
respect for cultural and group identity, and faith in social and political
institutions which enhance the participation of individuals and groups in
society. The underlying values and principles of a free and democratic society
are the genesis of the rights and freedoms guaranteed by the
Charter
and the
ultimate standard against which a limit on a right or freedom must be shown,
despite its effect, to be reasonable and demonstrably justified.

[
48
]

Creaghan J. went on to find that the thrust of s. 5 of the
Human
Rights Act
was of sufficient importance to warrant overriding Ross'
protected constitutional rights. At the same time the justice held that the
order of the board of inquiry met the test of proportionality, that is, that it
was reasonable and demonstrably justified to remove the teacher from the
class-room. In this respect, the judge in his decision on judicial review, held
that removal from the class-room was rationally connected to the objective of
rectifying the cause and effect of the violation of the
Human Rights Act.
Further,
he held that the order impaired as little as possible the constitutional rights
in question and that the effect of the order was proportional.

[
49
]

The judge came to a different conclusion, however, when he
applied the
Oakes

test to the termination of Ross' employment if he
should continue to publish, write or distribute his discriminatory works. He
held that that part of the order did not meet the test of proportionality and
that its rational connection to its objective was tenuous [at p. 758]:

Applying a rigorous application of the standard of proof by a
preponderance of probabilities, the respondents have failed to satisfy me that
cl. 2(d) of the order meets the test of proportionality. The rational
connection to the objective of s. 5 of the Act is tenuous, there is too great
an impairment of the constitutional rights in issue and I do not find that the
effect of this aspect of the order is reasonable and demonstrably justified
given the importance of s. 5 of the
Human Rights Act
within the factual
situation that arises in this instance.

[
50
]

With respect, I think Mr. Justice Creaghan's application of the
test applies equally to the ban on publication which has been referred to
throughout this case in argument as "the gag order". To sever the ban
order from the class-room situation simply does not answer the problem in a
meaningful way. It falls too short of the mark. The wrong is in the continued
discrimination publicly promoted by Ross, a public servant, as a role model to
children. He is known as an elementary schoolteacher whether in the classroom
or outside of it where he is promoting discrimination and prejudice. We cannot
in this age of pervasive mass communication, repetitious radio and television
news and public affairs programs, underestimate the cumulative effect on young
people of statements and writings made outside the class-room. They hear or see
the news before and after school. To draw the line at the class-room door is an
unrealistic barrier in this burgeoning age of information and communication. It
is to this end that the original ban order of Professor Bruce should be
reinstated.

In further support

[
51
]

It was not only the class-room conduct of Ross that was in
question. The complainant argued that the school board failed to provide equal
opportunity within the educational system on to respond to Ross' statements
made in public. Looking at the gravamen of the complaint, within and without
the class, Professor Bruce found a general failure on the part of the school
board to provide an environment and educational services to the public free of
discrimination.

Proportionality

[
52
]

The overall legislative objective is to ensure that the school
board does not discriminate with respect to providing educational services to
the public. In my opinion, the tripartite test which Mr. Justice Creaghan found
applicable to three of the four subsections of Professor Bruce's order applies
equally to all four. I will deal with each in turn as supplementary to his
reasons which I say uphold the four subsections of the order.

Rational connection

[
53
]

One must look at the discriminatory conduct to see whether there
is any affront to the guiding principles of the enabling legislation. Is the
order by Professor Bruce as a board of inquiry rationally connected to the aim
of furthering pressing and substantial objectives? According to counsel for the
Human Rights Commission, legislative objectives which have been held to meet
the pressing and substantial tests sufficient to limit a
Charter
right or
freedom include:

(a) The compelling interests of the province in the education
of the young may limit freedom of religion;

(b) An Order under labour legislation counteracting the
effects of an unjust dismissal may limit freedom of expression;

(c) The legislative suppression of wilful promotion of hatred
against identifiable groups may limit freedom of expression;

(d) State interest in a compulsory weekly day of rest may
limit freedom of religion;

(e) The legislative objective of promoting industrial peace
through encouragement of free collective bargaining and mandatory payment of
union dues may limit both freedom of expression and freedom of association;

(f) In the United States similar legislative objectives to
protect the union shop, and more generally the public welfare, may limit
freedom of religion;

(g) In the United States, the interest of an employer in
promoting the efficiency of public educational services may limit freedom of
expression.

[
54
]

I think that the order is rationally connected to the aim of
furthering pressing and substantial objectives. As pointed out by the Human
Rights Commission, the Act is conciliatory in nature and without criminal
sanction. It is well-suited to encourage reform of discriminatory conduct. The
order is therefore rationally connected to the objective of ensuring a
discrimination-free environment. This would further the overall legislative
intent.

Minimal impairment

[
55
]

I have already mentioned the near constitutional nature of human
rights legislation. The preamble to the Act recognizes a broad policy. It
purports to guarantee human rights by the rule of law. Professor Bruce gave
vent to this in his order.

[
56
]

By his interpretation of this remedial legislation, he was
advancing its broad policy, the basic goals and values of our society,
imperfect as they may be.

[
57
]

The Human Rights Commission contends that Professor Bruce could
have fashioned no less intrusive measures and still have achieved the objective
sought with any likelihood. According to the commission the aim of its
legislation is to prevent discriminatory effects and create remedial measures
compensatory and protective of the victim, rather than to stigmatize and punish
those who discriminate.

[
58
]

Professor Bruce considered and rejected numerous remedial
measures as being unsatisfactory such as apology and renunciation, continual
class-room monitoring, restricted access to class or school premises by pupils
on the basis of religion or ancestry, and monetary compensation.

[
59
]

As contended by the Human Rights Commission, the redeployment
order coupled with the restraint order tempers the harshness of an otherwise appropriate
order of outright dismissal. In support of this contention, the commission
points to American Supreme Court decisions in
Leary v. United States,
383
F.2d 851 (U.S.C.A., Fifth Circuit, 1967)
, and
Anderson v. Evans,
660 E2d
153 (U.S.C.A., Sixth Circuit, 1981), as well as to the remarks of Chief Justice
Dickson in
Slaight Communications Inc v. Davidson,
(1989)
1989 CanLII 92 (SCC)
, 59 D.L.R.
(4th) 416 at pp. 424-7, [1989] 1 S.C.R. 1038, 26 C.C.E.L. 85. The commission
argues that although freedom to believe is absolute, freedom to act upon one's
belief is conditional and relative, and may be proscribed and restricted in the
interests of the public welfare and the protection of society. American courts,
for example, sanction the outright dismissal of a public employee, including a
teacher, despite infringement upon freedom of expression.

[
60
]

A balance must be struck between Ross' freedoms, the victims'
freedoms and an educational system which teaches impartiality and does not
espouse prejudice, bigotry or bias. A teacher teaches. He is a role model. He
also teaches by example. Children learn by example. Malcolm Ross teaches by
example. He is a role model who publishes and promotes prejudice. This is
wrong.

[
61
]

In any event, the board of inquiry acted within its mandate and
determined, in the balancing of conflicting interests, to protect and improve
the conditions and interests of the disadvantaged and disempowered.

Deleterious effects

[
62
]

As contended by the Human Rights Commission, the rights and
freedoms specifically guaranteed by the
Charter
, including those of speech and
religion, may be measured against the underlying values and principles of a
free and democratic society which are their very genesis, and limited where to
do so furthers those values and principles. Included in these are the inherent
dignity of the human being, commitment to social justice and equality and
respect for cultural and group identity. To give free reign to the asserted
freedom of speech and religion of Ross would be to trample upon these
underlying values and principles, themselves having the status of entrenched
rights under the Charter and in international law.

[
63
]

Ross remains free to leave public employment and engage fully in
the exercise of his freedom of speech and religion without restraint. A
restriction, therefore, that he cease his discriminatory conduct is a
justifiable infringement. It is not absolute.

[
64
]

The primary goal of the order is to remedy the effects upon the
victims of discriminatory conduct engaged in by the appellant Ross contrary to
the
Human Rights Act
The sanction imposed upon him is minimal and, in my
opinion, its effects are not so deleterious as to outweigh the objectives of
the measures.

[
65
]

Accordingly, I would dismiss the appeal and allow, in part, the
cross-appeals of the Human Rights Commission, David Attis and the Canadian
Jewish Congress, by reinstating s-s. (d), the ban on publication which had been
quashed by Mr. Justice Creaghan. The respondents who entered cross-appeals are
each entitled to costs of $1,000. Each of the other respondents who were
represented on the appeal is entitled to costs of $300.

[
66
]

Appeal allowed; cross-appeals dismissed.
